newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australis says ad revenue some way off.
newsitem.headline: Australis says ad revenue some way off.

text.p: The potential for pay television advertising in Australia is over-stated and it will be several years before it becomes a meaningful revenue stream, Australis Media Ltd chief executive Sean O'Halloran said on Sunday.
"I think that the potential for pay television advertising is a little over-stated at the current time," O'Halloran said.
"I think that it will take a number of years for that to become a meaninful revenue stream for pay television in Australia," he said in a television interview.
"I think it will be a nice earner maybe over the course of five to ten years, but as of today I wouldn't be resting the success of my business on the inflow of advertising revenues."
Australis is one of three major pay-tv operators in Australia and the only one that is listed on the stock exchange.

The other operators are Optus Vision, owned by Optus Communications Pty Ltd, Australia's second biggest telecommunications company, and Foxtel, owned by The News Corp Ltd and state-owned telecoms carrier Telstra Corp.
The three have racked up a total loss of about A$1.5 billion since 1993 when satellite tv operator Australis was formed.
Australis is due to report results for the nine months to March 31 in the next few days.

The interview with O'Halloran was recorded before the Supreme Court of New South Wales on Friday ruled against a proposed joint infrastructure venture between Australis and Optus Vision under which Australis would transfer its satellite infrastructure to a joint venture with Optus Vision.
The action was started Foxtel, which has a 25-year programming deal with Australis.
The satellite deal was seen as an important part of the recapitalisation of Australis last year.
O'Halloran said the current picture for rationalisation of pay tv in Australia was complex. "I think it is a fair characterisation to say that everybody's talking to everybody."

He said pay TV had a market penetration of between 11 and 13 percent. "I think that you'll see significant advertising revenues pay as a category when penetration levels are closer to 30, 40, 50 percent than 11 to 13 percent," he said.
O'Halloran said the Australian market could in theory support two or three operators.

"I don't think that it's a question so much of how many operators, I think that industry rationalisation is not about reducing the number of players necessarily from three to two, or even from two to one," he said.

"Industry rationalisation is, I think, a euphemism for discontinuing wasteful infrastructure duplication which is half of the heart of the problem and a euphemism for reducing programme costs which is the other half of the problem."
Australis shares closed unchanged at 15 cents on Friday.
